For instance if we drag "fire" element onto "glacier" location then we produce water. Note that neither A nor B nor the new element C are in any way tied to the location. For instance if the goal is "put a receiver on the high ridge" then it is satisfied by dragging the receiver onto the high ridge.

At the end of the day our two guides said to the ten of us, "okay, good bye" and left us for the night. The ten of us looked at each other. We lay down on the ground. We were freezing cold, in October in the high desert in Utah. We were mostly men and didn't want to cuddle for warmth. We tried putting a few pathetic branches for warmth but it didn't work. At 2am we woke up from the cold, saw that our nalgene watter bottles were FROZEN COMPLETELY SOLID, and just climbed up and down the hill to stay warm.
2. On the second day, after dawn, the guides re-appeared and said hello. We walked all day. They told us to pick a stone for our hands, and grind a hole in it. We did that while sitting for a break at lunchtime. (No food yesterday, no food today). At night we crossed a small stream and stayed the night in a cave on the sandy river bank shore. Once again the guides left. This time we all slept together, like sardines, rotating whose turn it was on the outside.
3. On the third day the guides met us again. We walked. They had us find suitable sticks, and taught us how to whittle a spoon, and a firestick. Everyone was getting fed up. That evening  towards the end of the day's hike they pulled a little prank on us "look, these reeds show that ants have stung the tubers underground", and revealed our supplies -- a wool blanket, 1000 calories a day of outmeal and flour and milk poweder and raisins and carrots and potatoes. That night we cooked a simple meal, ate with the wooden spoon we each whittled, and slept with our blankets.
4. On subsequent days they taught us how to stay warm. Gather dry leaves about 4' deep. Slide yourself into them. That way we'll be warmer than even a thick duvet. They taught us how to start fires with the "bow" method, using the stick and stone that we'd prepared. They taught us about tinder, punked wood, keeping a little pouch of our fire starters and maybe keeping a glowing ember in our pouch. They taught us how to set traps for animals, and how small animals like toasted nuts (a delicious smell which they can never create themselves in nature). We caught a rat, but we were so scared of plague and fleas that we cooked it basically to charcoal so it wasn't very good eating. They taught us how to weave sticks into a fish trap.
5. One on day they brought a lamb, and taught us how to slaughter it, process it, wash its stomach in the river and use the stomach to cook a boiled pudding (flour, dough, raisins inside, which steam delightfully). We made pemican, jerky, all kinds of things with every part of the animal.
6. Some of us stored our carrots in our water bottles to keep them fresh. Some of us picked mint, or juniper berries, for flavor. (I know LOATHE the taste of juniper berries!) They taught us about crypto vegetation, hidden black starts of life in the desert sands. Small desert onions. They taught us never to pick more than two out of five plants that we see, so there is always some left.
6. For three days they left us completely in solitary, with about 3 miles between each of us. We had to do shelter, fire, scout out our area, pass the time, reflect, all by ourselves.
7. One day we saw a high up cave where the native americans had kept their stores. We watched the ravens fly by and learned about raven cloaks.
8. On the last evening they led us to a nice cave and this time they brought food from their course garden, and cooked a nice dinner for us. We slept in the cave. They woke us up at 2am and told us that the base was "in that direction" and each of us ran or walked, solo, under the wheeling stars (there was no moon). Somehow I knew the way. Running over the red earth, judging time by how the stars had wheeled over the mountain's silhouette. It was like a dream.
9. We returned to the base. They had a native american style sweat lodge, where we gathered and talked.

There's a second follow-up course which I never did, "Hunter Gatherer". In that 2-week course you're not given any food at all, and have to find it all yourself in the utah high desert. Escalante was the name of that region. My friend did the course. On the first day they guided him to finding a gourd which he hollowed out to carry water. He got food poisoning and had diarrhea and didn't have a great time. But he made it. There's an old saying about how to learn how to be a hunter: "the best teacher is hunger".
